title: A critical potassium on a medical unit

bedside.infusions: KCl 10 mEq/h: {kclOn ? "running" : "stopped"}. Dextrose 10%: {d10On ? "50 mL/h" : "off"}. Calcium doses: {calDoses}.

banner.text: Monitor: wide QRS complexes, rate slowing.

banner.when: monitorOn and risk < wideRisk and kNow >= 6.5

objective: Identify hyperkalemia -- serum potassium above 5.1 mEq/L -- by irritability, cramping, diarrhea and peaked T waves, and know it can progress to dysrhythmia and cardiac arrest
secondaryObjectives: Medical emergencies: applying pathophysiology under time pressure
Testing within the nurse's scope: ECG, point-of-care testing, fetal monitoring
Evaluating the client's response to a medication over time
Unexpected adverse response to therapy, and recognizing complications early
Prevent medication errors through the safety checks in four groups: identify the client correctly, check the order for errors, keep the environment safe, and monitor for adverse reactions

sources.note: Relayed from the REQ-233 NCLEX-RN cases (read 2026-11-11, primary PDF), not re-read: Physiological Adaptation includes managing a medical emergency and fluid and electrolyte imbalances; Reduction of Risk Potential includes recognizing changes in laboratory values and performing an ECG within scope; Pharmacological Therapies includes evaluating the client's response to medication.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

brief.situation: 08:40 on a medical unit. You are Mr. Hutchins' RN. The lab phones a critical result: potassium 6.8 mEq/L on the 07:30 draw (no hemolysis noted). Mr. Hutchins, 71, says his legs feel heavy and he has felt sick since breakfast.
handover: Admitted two days ago with cellulitis of the left leg; chronic kidney disease stage 4. About 80 kg.
Yesterday's potassium was 3.4 after IV furosemide, so potassium chloride 10 mEq/h IV was ordered 'until four runs are done'. The third run is infusing now.
Home medicines restarted yesterday: lisinopril 20 mg and spironolactone 25 mg, both due at 09:00.
Not on telemetry. Glucose was 92 mg/dL at 07:30.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Orders for medicines come from the hospitalist after you call. Results take time to come back.
Partway through you are asked to write what is happening and why. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Potassium climbs about 0.75 mEq/L an hour while the KCl runs into failing kidneys, and about 0.25 an hour once it stops (spironolactone, lisinopril, CKD). FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
See riseOn. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Giving the 09:00 spironolactone and lisinopril adds a further rise over the case. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

why.question: What is happening, why, and what comes first? What could go wrong with the treatment itself?

parts.label: Recognition
parts.criteria: Names severe hyperkalemia (6.8, above 6.5) with ECG changes (peaked T waves), weakness and GI symptoms; links it to the KCl infusion into CKD 4 plus spironolactone and lisinopril; knows it can progress to wide QRS, bradycardia and arrest.
parts.modelAnswer: Severe hyperkalemia: 6.8 with peaked T waves, heavy legs, nausea and loose stools. Potassium is running into kidneys that can't clear it, and spironolactone and lisinopril hold it in. Next comes a wide QRS, a slow rhythm and arrest.

parts.label: Priorities and risks
parts.criteria: Stop the KCl, monitor and 12-lead, call with the value and ECG; calcium first to protect the heart (lasts 30-60 min, repeat if changes persist), then insulin with dextrose to shift K in, albuterol as an add-on; hold the spironolactone and lisinopril; glucose before insulin and at 30 and 60 min, dextrose infusion because glucose is under 126, because insulin can cause hypoglycemia; recheck K at 1 h.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop the KCl, monitor and 12-lead, call the hospitalist with the number and the ECG. Calcium gluconate first: it protects the heart within minutes but wears off in under an hour. Insulin with dextrose moves potassium into cells; albuterol helps alongside. Hold his 09:00 spironolactone and lisinopril. The risk of the treatment is hypoglycemia: check glucose first, run dextrose 10% since he's under 126, and check at 30 and 60 minutes. Recheck potassium an hour after the insulin.

noProgress.rationale: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes still untreated or unchecked two hours after a critical call leaves him at risk of arrest, so this case calls it harm.

source.note: Read 2026-11-14 in the primary PDF through a summarizing fetch with quotes: severe hyperkalaemia is 6.5 mmol/L or more (mmol/L and mEq/L are equal for potassium); at least continuous 3-lead ECG monitoring at 6.5 or more (14.2); peaked T waves, flattened P waves and wide QRS, then bradycardia, sine wave and VT; step 1 IV calcium, '30ml 10% Calcium Gluconate over 10 minutes', effective 'within 3 minutes', 'duration of action is only 30-60 minutes', repeat if ECG changes persist (16.2); '10 units soluble insulin in 25g glucose' (16.3.1), K 'starts to fall within 15 minutes', 'peak reduction (ranging from 0.65-1.0 mmol/l) occurring between 30-60 minutes', sustained up to 2 hours; hypoglycaemia in 8-28%; if pre-treatment glucose is below 7.0 mmol/L, '10% glucose at a rate of 50ml/hour for 5 hours' (16.3.3); glucose at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, 300 and 360 minutes (17.2); nebulised salbutamol 10-20 mg as an adjunct, never alone, onset within 30 minutes, 10 mg lowers K by 0.53-0.88 (16.4); bicarbonate not routine (16.5); K at least 1, 2, 4, 6 and 24 h after treatment (17.1.2); remove the cause (step 5).

expertPath.text: Read back the critical value. Stop the KCl. Look at him: weak legs, nausea, loose stools.
Monitor on: peaked T waves. Start a 12-lead. Check his glucose (92). Call the hospitalist with K 6.8, the ECG, the KCl, CKD 4, spironolactone and lisinopril.
Calcium gluconate over 10 minutes; insulin 10 units with 25 g dextrose; dextrose 10% at 50 mL/h because he is under 126; albuterol. Hold the 09:00 spironolactone and lisinopril.
Glucose checks. Potassium recheck an hour after the insulin. Document.

arrest.headline: Cardiac arrest
arrest.body: Severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes needs the potassium source stopped, calcium to protect the heart, and a shift into cells, within minutes.

seizure.headline: The treatment caused severe hypoglycemia
seizure.body: Insulin lowers glucose as well as potassium. With a pre-treatment glucose under 126, run dextrose 10% and check glucose at 30 and 60 minutes.

stable.headline: Severe hyperkalemia treated safely
stable.body: You stopped the source, protected the heart with calcium, shifted potassium with insulin, dextrose and albuterol, held the potassium-raising medicines, and watched his glucose. That is the expert path.

stableLate.headline: Potassium down, by a slower or riskier route
stableLate.body: Look at when the KCl stopped, when the call landed, when calcium went in, and how his glucose was watched.

time_up.headline: Not treated in time
time_up.body: A critical potassium with ECG changes is an emergency: stop the source, call with the number and the rhythm, calcium, then a shift.

scoring.modelReasoning: A potassium of 6.8 with peaked T waves, weakness and GI symptoms is severe hyperkalemia; here it comes from potassium chloride running into stage 4 CKD, made worse by spironolactone and lisinopril. Untreated it widens the QRS, slows the rhythm and stops the heart. Stop the KCl, put him on a monitor, do a 12-lead, and call the hospitalist with the value, the ECG and the causes. Calcium gluconate comes first: it protects the heart within about 3 minutes but lasts only 30 to 60 minutes and is repeated if ECG changes persist. Insulin with dextrose moves potassium into cells (falling within 15 minutes, lowest at 30 to 60), and albuterol is an add-on, never alone. The treatment's own risk is hypoglycemia: check glucose first, run dextrose 10% at 50 mL/h when the pre-treatment glucose is under 126 mg/dL, and check at 30 and 60 minutes. Hold the potassium-raising medicines, recheck potassium an hour after treatment, and document.

calQ.ask: While the hospitalist calls back: which treatment protects his heart first?
calQ.explain: IV calcium stabilizes the heart within about 3 minutes but does not lower potassium; insulin with dextrose lowers it; bicarbonate is not routine.

choices.label: Up to 6 hours: 0, 30, 60, 90, 120 minutes, then hourly
